1.pericope_label: The command to number Israel, and why

schools.summary: Gill names the wilderness of Sinai from the mountain of the decalogue and reckons eleven months of encampment there, reports Aben Ezra's reason that the standards had to be fixed because the march began on the twentieth of that month. Calvin argues that this was really the second numbering, since a tax had already been imposed on every person, and that it was ordered because the camp was about to move, a third following later to show how a new generation had preserved the people's numbers; he insists that Israel was never numbered except at God's command, so that He might assert His supreme dominion, and that the tribal superintendents were appointed to keep any man from slipping into a tribe not his own.

Henry places the commission at God's court in the wilderness, issued from the royal palace of the tabernacle in what may be called the second year of that reign, and gives four reasons for it — to prove the promise to Abraham fulfilled, since seventy-five souls had become hundreds of thousands in two hundred and fifteen years; to show the care God takes of Israel as a shepherd counting his flock; to distinguish true-born Israelites from the mixed multitude; and to marshal a body which without mustering would be a rout and a rabble. He observes that none under twenty were taken, God in compassion to their tender years refusing to arm them, that the militant church reckons as members only those enlisted as soldiers of Christ, and that the honourable should study to be serviceable.

Clarke infers from the two dates that everything in the preceding book happened within a single month at Sinai, adds to the reasons for the census that families might be so distinguished as to prevent future litigation over inheritance and that the Messiah's descent through the house of David might be traceable, and lists those excluded — women, children, strangers, old men and the Levites, who alone amounted to more than twenty-two thousand. Wesley reckons a full year in the wilderness, and separates this muster from the earlier one, which preceded the tabernacle and served to tax the people for its charges, passing on the conjecture that the Levites were counted then and excepted now.

Ellicott notes that the tent of meeting had been set up a month before, takes the earlier reckoning to have been made six months previously by counting the half-shekels paid, observes that its total exactly matches this one, and argues that since both sums and all the items are divisible by ten no objection to either record can stand if those coming of age balanced the deaths — while preferring the supposition that there was only one census; he glosses the polls as heads counted man by man and the clan as including several fathers' houses. Keil and Delitzsch frame the book as the road from Sinai to Canaan preparing Israel for possession as the road from Goshen to Sinai had prepared them for the covenant, explain fathers' houses as the standing term for the subdivisions of each tribe's families, and identify the man assigned from every tribe as its prince.

debates: Whether this is the first census or a repetition. Calvin makes it the second, the earlier tax-count being the first, with a third to come; Wesley separates the two musters by date, occasion and purpose; Ellicott, having noted that the totals agree exactly, prefers to suppose there was only one census throughout.

How the identical totals are to be explained. Wesley passes on the conjecture that the Levites were included earlier and excepted here, their number replaced by those newly of age; Ellicott appeals to the divisibility of every figure by ten and to a rough balance of deaths against those coming of age.

Why the numbering was ordered. Henry gives four reasons, Clarke adds inheritance litigation and the Messiah's genealogy, Gill reports Aben Ezra's practical one about fixing the standards for the march, and Calvin makes the point one of divine dominion rather than administration.
outliers: Clarke's inference that the whole of the preceding book falls within one month, since the tabernacle was raised on the first of the first month and this muster ordered on the first of the second.
Henry's image of God as the shepherd who keeps count of his flock.
Calvin's note that a third numbering was taken before the entry into Canaan, so that comparison might show a new generation making up the losses.
themes: a muster at the foot of Sinai

5.pericope_label: The twelve princes named to assist

schools.summary: Gill insists the twelve stood with Moses and Aaron as working assistants rather than spectators or auditors, each best acquainted with the families of his own tribe, and stresses that they were named by the Lord himself rather than chosen by Moses or elected by their tribes, which he counts a great honour; he takes the renowned for the most eminent by birth or by wisdom and courage, prefers the rendering the called of the congregation, and passes on Aben Ezra's remark that the congregation did nothing until it had called them and Jarchi's that they were summoned to every business of importance.

Wesley states the principle on which the tribes are ordered, the children of Leah first, then Rachel's, then the handmaids', and disposes of the Deuel–Reuel crux by noting that the two Hebrew letters are often interchanged. Clarke sets the same order out as a table by mother and seniority, and treats the name at length — marshalling the Greek and Syriac against the Vulgate, Samaritan and Arabic, with many manuscripts and a third passage, to conclude that Deuel was the original reading; he also reports the rabbinic solution that Eliasaph was a proselyte, son of Reuel before his conversion and of Deuel after, and suspects it was built on the two words meaning the breach of God and the knowledge of God. He gives the renowned the literal sense of those summoned by name to attend.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew reads for Reuben rather than of the tribe of Reuben, expands the called men of the congregation into a standing office — representatives of their tribes appointed to act in regulating the affairs of the nation — and would render the last phrase they were the heads of the thousands of Israel, comparing the princes of thousands recommended by Jethro and appointed by Moses as the highest class of officers. Keil and Delitzsch record simply that the command was carried out, the twelve heads of tribes being taken as they had been designated by name.

debates: Whether the father of Gad's prince was Deuel or Reuel. Clarke weighs the versions and manuscripts and decides for Deuel as original, the two Hebrew letters being nearly identical; Wesley notes the same interchange without adjudicating.

What the renowned means. Gill allows eminence of birth or character but prefers the called of the congregation; Clarke gives the same literal sense of men summoned by name; Ellicott makes it a formal representative office.
outliers: The rabbinic solution reported by Clarke, that Eliasaph was a proselyte called son of Reuel before his conversion and son of Deuel after, apparently grounded on the two names meaning the breach of God and the knowledge of God.
Gill's point that the twelve were named by God himself rather than chosen by Moses or elected by their tribes.

17.pericope_label: The muster carried out, and the twelve tribal numbers

schools.summary: Gill dates the assembly to Ijar, answering to part of April and May, on the very day the word came, contrasts Moses numbering by express command and in obedience with David numbering without one and against his will, and explains that the tribes are taken in the order of their encampment rather than of birth, Simeon and Gad following Reuben because they stood under his standard. Calvin meets the objection that one family could not increase so far in two hundred and fifty years by answering that an increase depending on God's power cannot be measured by ordinary rules and that the Spirit means to exhibit a signal miracle; he reads Reuben's comparatively small numbers as marks of the curse and his degradation from the firstborn's honours, and Judah's pre-eminence as the blessing already calling that tribe to primogeniture and supremacy.

Henry notes that the work began the same day it was ordered, since what is to be done for God should be set about while the sense of duty is strong, and contrasts it with Joab's ten months for David — a dispersed people against a compact one, a muster proposed by Satan against one commanded by God. He observes that the numbers stand in words at length and the formula is repeated for each tribe, showing a single rule and method and letting every man know his next of kin; he prefers to explain the round totals by Moses' earlier rulers of hundreds and fifties rather than by special providence; he refers Judah's pre-eminence to the descent of the Messiah and to its leading the van, Ephraim's precedence to Jacob's crossed hands, and the reversal between Dan and Benjamin to the truth that families do not increase or diminish by probabilities; and he takes the refrain about going forth to war as a warning that he who girds on the harness should not boast as though he had put it off.

Wesley judges the numbering to have taken a single day, notes that Judah far exceeds every other tribe in accomplishment of Jacob's prophecy, recalls the devil's vain attempt to defeat that promise through the men of Gath, and draws from Dan's growth against Benjamin's the lesson that God makes such changes easily and often, so that none should please themselves in a numerous offspring. Clarke passes on Ainsworth's remark that Gad alone ends in fifty while the rest end in hundreds, as showing providence in the increase, and presses the fulfilment of the prophecy that the younger brother should be greater, since no word of God can fall to the ground.

Ellicott renders the declaration of pedigrees as announcing themselves to have been born, that is, causing themselves to be enrolled, sets out the three heads of the enrolment — tribe, family running in some cases to two or three thousand persons, and father's house — stresses the importance of such a register as a means of tracing the genealogy of Christ, and notes both Judah's superiority and Ephraim's excess over Manasseh in connection with the patriarchal blessings.

debates: Why the totals are round. Clarke, following Ainsworth, sees providence in the absence of any broken number; Henry reports that view but prefers the administrative explanation, that the people were counted through the rulers of hundreds and fifties appointed earlier.

How far the figures may be pressed against nature. Calvin refuses to measure by ordinary rules an increase that depended on God's power, and treats the objection as missing the Spirit's intention to exhibit a miracle.

What the disparities between tribes signify. Calvin reads Reuben's smallness as the visible mark of his lost primogeniture and Judah's size as the blessing of Genesis 49; Henry, Wesley, Clarke and Ellicott all connect Judah's and Ephraim's numbers with the patriarchal prophecies.
outliers: Henry's contrast between this muster and Joab's, one commanded by God and the other proposed by Satan.
Ellicott's observation that the value of the enrolment lies partly in its providing the means of tracing the genealogy of Christ.
Wesley's note that the devil tried in vain to defeat Ephraim's promised increase by stirring up the men of Gath.
themes: a census done in a day
a register read against the blessings
able to go forth to war

44.pericope_label: The sum total, six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty

schools.summary: Gill observes that the total exactly matches the count taken seven months earlier for the tabernacle assessment, so that apparently no one had died, the three recorded violent deaths not touching the figure since two were Levites and the third the son of a non-Israelite father; thinking it improbable that no man above twenty died among so many, he reports the alternative that Levi was included before and excepted now, the increase in the other tribes making up the difference.

Henry takes the unchanged total to show that whatever we part with for the honour and service of God is certainly made up to us one way or other, and puts three questions to the number: what it cost to maintain such a body for forty years in a wilderness, with twice as many women, children, sick and aged besides, all fed daily from the dew of heaven rather than the fatness of the earth, so that God appears as a great and good housekeeper; what work sin makes with a people, since by unbelief and murmuring every man numbered here but two laid his bones in the wilderness; and what a multitude God's spiritual Israel will prove at last, a little flock in one place and time but innumerable when gathered.

Clarke marvels at the increase from seventy souls in two hundred and fifteen years of hardship, sets the book's two censuses side by side in decreasing order, notes that except Gad here and Reuben later every figure is round because Scripture disregards units and fractions, reads off Judah as the most populous and Manasseh the least by more than forty-two thousand without being able to assign a reason, observes that in the second census Simeon has fallen from third to smallest with seven tribes increasing and five declining, and reproduces Scheuchzer's arithmetical derivation of the totals from four Egyptian generations while printing alongside it the objection that it allots Dan's families some fifty-three children each against Benjamin's nineteen.
Ellicott notes that the odd numbers were not reckoned at all, the whole being given roundly elsewhere as six hundred thousand.

debates: Why the total is unchanged from the earlier count. Gill and Henry both report the explanation that Levi was numbered before and excepted now, the other tribes' increase filling the gap; Gill adds that the recorded deaths of the interval do not affect the figure, but doubts that no man above twenty died among so many.

How much weight the figures will bear. Clarke defends Scheuchzer's derivation as natural and confirmed by each tribe's total, yet prints the objection that its family sizes are wildly uneven; Ellicott simply observes that odd numbers were never reckoned.
outliers: Clarke's note that Judah exceeds Manasseh by more than forty-two thousand, for which he can give no satisfactory reason.
Clarke's observation that Simeon, third largest here, is the smallest of all tribes by the second census.
Henry's image of God as a housekeeper feeding such a household daily from the dew of heaven rather than the fatness of the earth.
themes: seventy souls become six hundred thousand

47.pericope_label: The Levites exempted, and charged with the tabernacle

schools.summary: Gill explains that the Levites were already engaged in a kind of warfare and so not to be drawn into another, notes that the exception is stated expressly lest Moses be thought to have spared his own tribe from affection, and qualifies it carefully — they were not forbidden war and might undertake it willingly at need, as the Maccabees did, but could not be compelled, an exemption always allowed to those in religious service; he places their tents between the tabernacle and the camps and compares the four living creatures about the throne, and closes on the people's ready and punctual obedience. Calvin insists that Moses acted at God's bidding rather than from ambition for his own tribe, faults the usual rendering of the following verse, reads the restriction on handling the tabernacle as enforcing its sanctity and reminding all Israel of its unworthiness to approach, denies that the honour gave the tribe any ground of boasting since it rested on God's good pleasure alone, and finds in the arrangement an image of the priesthood of Christ, assuring believers that the Mediator would be of the human race.

Henry treats the exemption as an honour earned in the matter of the golden calf, singular services being recompensed with singular honours, and observes that as a holy people was not reckoned among the nations so a holy tribe was not reckoned among other Israelites, their own service being called a warfare which discharged them from this one. He divides their charge between the march and the camp — taking down, carrying and setting up the tabernacle, then encamping round it as a guard against plunder and profanation — holds that the holy things were honoured by being kept from all but those called of God, applies this to our own unfitness for fellowship with God until grace calls us into the fellowship of his Son, states that preventing sin is preventing wrath, and admonishes ministers to distinguish themselves by aiming to be really better rather than to seem greater.

Wesley explains the exemption by the purpose of the muster, which had war in view while the Levites were to attend the tabernacle, and draws the rule that those who minister upon holy things should not entangle themselves in secular affairs since the ministry is work enough for a whole man; he derives the name tabernacle of testimony from the ark it was chiefly made for, takes the stranger to mean a man of another tribe rather than another nation, and describes the wrath in question as that of a God tender of his worship, called simply wrath by way of eminence as the most terrible kind.

Ellicott prefers the rendering And the Lord spake, and observes that although the Levites must have been exempted by divine direction nothing here points back to an earlier command nor had their destination yet been declared; he traces the title tabernacle of testimony to the tables of the law in the ark, which give ark, tabernacle, tent and veil alike that name, likens the tent of meeting to a royal palace with the Levites as its guard of honour, glosses the stranger as one not of the tribe of Levi, and takes the word for wrath to denote an immediate visitation of God's hand such as a plague.

debates: Whether the verse looks back to an earlier command. Calvin argues that it must, since omitting a whole tribe would be absurd unless God's will had already been declared, and blames the translators for obscuring it; Ellicott adopts the same rendering but denies that any previous command about the Levites is in view.

How far the exemption from war extended. Gill holds that the Levites were exempt from compulsion but not forbidden to fight, citing the Maccabees; Wesley and Henry treat the exemption as flowing from the nature of their own service, which was itself a warfare.
What the stranger means here. Ellicott and Wesley agree that the word denotes a man of another tribe rather than a foreigner, contrary to its ordinary use.
outliers: Calvin's argument that the honour conferred on Levi was a testimony of gratuitous favour and an image of the priesthood of Christ, assuring believers that the Mediator would be of the human race.
Gill's comparison of the Levites' encampment with the four living creatures about the throne.
Ellicott's picture of the tent of meeting as a royal palace guarded by a guard of honour.
themes: a tribe left out of the muster
a guard set round the holy things
